vignette:
Marcus

Marcus sits in the leather chair with his shoulders slightly hunched, fingers interlaced in his lap. At seventy-two, he still carries the posture of someone accustomed to hunching over a keyboard, though he retired five years ago. His silver hair is neatly trimmed, and he wears a pressed button-down shirt despite the casual nature of the session. There's a precision to how he arranges himself—everything deliberate, controlled.

He was thirty-seven when it happened. A software engineer with a young company, Marcus had been recruited to help establish a tech infrastructure initiative in a Central American country. He believed in the work—democratizing access to information, he'd told friends. In 1989, he was detained at a checkpoint while traveling to a remote facility. The soldiers thought he was someone else, or perhaps they didn't care who he was. For eleven days, he was held in a concrete room with a single window too high to see from. He was beaten. He was interrogated about information he didn't possess. He was subjected to near-drowning. On the twelfth day, a mistake was corrected, an official intervened, and he was released.

He returned to the United States and never spoke about those eleven days with anyone—not his family, not his colleagues, not the few romantic partners who came and went over the decades. He worked. He coded. He built systems that processed millions of transactions. Work was the architecture that held him together.

For decades, Marcus functioned. But functionality, he's learning now, is not the same as living. The nightmares began in earnest about three years ago, though he traces their roots further back—to the quality of his sleep always being somehow wrong, his dreams always carrying an edge of dread. Now they come several times a week. He wakes gasping, his sheets soaked through, sometimes not sure which decade he's in. The bedroom feels unsafe, so he sleeps in the living room now, in his recliner, where he can see the door.

Loud noises startle him violently. A car backfiring sent him to the floor of his garage last month. He avoids crowds, which wasn't difficult to arrange—retirement and age naturally narrowed his world. But even small gatherings at the grocery store can leave him feeling exposed, scanning faces, assessing exits. He's aware this isn't rational. The engineer in him recognizes the pattern as faulty logic, but recognition doesn't stop the body's response.

What troubles him most now is the numbness. He moved through his career building connections with colleagues, but those relationships were always surface-level. Since retiring, he hasn't maintained friendships. He has a sister in Seattle he speaks to twice a year. He has no one he sees regularly. When he tries to imagine activities he once enjoyed—hiking, reading fiction—they feel impossibly distant, as if he's observing someone else's life through glass.

He's also developed what he calls "the checks." Before bed, he checks that all doors are locked three times. Before leaving his apartment, he checks them again. He's aware this is excessive. He's aware it provides only temporary relief. But the checking has become a necessary ritual, a way of imposing order on an internal chaos he cannot quite name.

Marcus describes all of this matter-of-factly, like he's debugging code, identifying the corrupted lines. But there's a weariness beneath the technical language—the exhaustion of someone who has been running a background process for over thirty years, and who is only now beginning to acknowledge the system is failing.
